blocks.c: Far Side, caveman can't pronounce pterodactyl

blocks.x: You may still remember the moment in grade school when your mind was blown after learning that “pterodactyl” was actually pronounced without the “p” sound, for no apparent reason. You may have even gone on to struggle to pronounce the word whenever you came across it in your science book, with your mind unable to accept that a word beginning with “pt” would have no “p” sound whatsoever.
Well, according to Larson, this isn’t just a modern-day problem. Even the cavemen of the past had trouble pronouncing the word: “Look out, Thak! It’s a ... a Dang! Never can pronounce those things!”

Next up is another comic where primitive times collide with modernity. This strip also adds Larson poking fun at the cavemen's intelligence, another recurring element in his caveman-centric strips. Here, two cavemen play an early version of checkers. For those unaware, checkers is a game played on a 64-square board, with 12 round playing pieces allotted to each player. The ultimate goal is to move across the board while capturing your opponent’s pieces.

In Larson’s strip, however, there are only two squares and two pieces. So when one of the cavemen thinks, “Oh, wait! I don’t want to do that!” it becomes a visual gag at the expense of the two cavemen’s intelligence.

blocks.c: far side cavemen invent the wheel comic

blocks.x: Larson’s “Early Experiments in Transportation” is another strip that relies heavily on visual gag humor. History buffs know the invention of the wheel was revolutionary for humans, serving as one of humanity’s most important technological breakthroughs thanks to its impact on transportation, trade, construction, and more.

Here, Larson pokes a little fun at this early invention, specifically its uses in transportation. In his instantly recognizable style, he depicts a caveman tied to the “tread” of a wheel atop a hill. The implication is clear: the cavemen intend to push him down the hill. However, the viewer has the foresight the cavemen lack, making it painfully obvious that this will end in a failed transportation experiment.

One defining aspect of modern life is our individual hobbies. In fact, many people tie their identity to their recreational pursuits, sometimes even more so than their chosen careers. We don’t typically ponder what hobbies may have existed during prehistoric times, given that, for the most part, hobbies didn’t really exist because humans were too busy trying to survive.

However, Larson circumvents this in his strip by exploring what hobbies may have been available to humans during the caveman era, and, well, let’s just say there wasn’t much variety. You could either pursue a rock collection or... pursue a rock collection.

blocks.c: The Far Side caveman kills duck out of envy

blocks.x: This next caveman strip stands out from the other additions on the list because it takes a step back from The Far Side’s defining humor and instead puts the spotlight on a harsh truth about humanity. The strip depicts a caveman watching a duck fly overhead. When the caveman sees the bird soaring through the sky, he begins flapping his arms, trying to fly himself.

Eventually, accepting that he cannot fly, the caveman fashions a bow and arrow and uses it to shoot the bird down, killing it. There is no punchline. Instead, it conveys one of the darkest truths about the human condition: envy. So, while there is no humor here, the profoundness of this strip makes it more than deserving of its place on this list of the best caveman comics from The Far Side.

blocks.c: A caveman is used like a plow in Far Side Comics

blocks.x: To make up for the darkness of the previous strip, this comic is pure hilarity. Combining both visual gag humor and a clever play on words, Larson depicts Caveman A holding Caveman B by the ankles, with Caveman B’s face being pushed through the dirt in a forward motion.

While this is already a humorous image, it’s the caption that delivers the hilarious punchline: “Barrow,” a precursor to the game of “wheelbarrow.” The joke is imagining what the game of “wheelbarrow” looked like before the invention of the wheel.

Here's another joke imagining what a classic game would have looked like before certain inventions. This strip imagines what “Rock, Paper, Scissors” would have looked like in the caveman era, and since there was no paper or scissors, the game simply would have been “rock... rock... rock.”

The strip is captioned “Before paper and scissors” and depicts three cavemen playing the primitive version of the game, with one of the cavemen exclaiming, “Dang it! Tied again! Ready... one, two, three!” The fact that the cavemen haven’t figured out that there can be no winner in a game of “rock, rock, rock” also pokes fun at their intelligence, adding to the humor.

In a world defined by human greed and what often feels like unnecessary taxes and charges, this Far Side comic hits surprisingly close to home. Here, Larson depicts the invention of the wheel and the subsequent invention of the parking meter.

The joke hits close to home because Larson suggests that every advancement designed to make life easier will eventually become another opportunity to charge us for the privilege of using it. The wheel makes transportation easier, but the parking meter ensures that even that convenience comes with a price. It’s a clever jab at the seemingly endless taxes, fees, and charges that define human life.

blocks.c: Dead caveman far side and drawings

blocks.x: This Far Side comic depicts two archaeologists as they stumble upon the remains of a caveman speared through the chest, along with his cave painting. The male archaeologist exclaims, “Amazing! The mummified remains of a prehistoric cave-painter, still clutching his brush! Seems he made an enemy, though.”

The humor comes from the cave painting, as we learn exactly what the cave painter did to make an enemy: he drew the face of the man who would eventually become his murderer on the rear end of a wild beast. This is classic Larson gag humor and remains one of his most underrated caveman comics.

blocks.c: A caveman teaching other cavemen about the 'Thagomizer'.

blocks.x: Topping our list is perhaps the most famous caveman-starring comic of all time. This comic depicts a classroom full of cavemen learning the terminology for different parts of dinosaurs. Here, the teacher introduces the terminology for the spikes on a dinosaur’s tail: “Now, this end is called the thagomizer after the late Thag Simmons.”

blocks.c: The Far Side's version of God

blocks.x: Among Gary Larson’s thought-provoking strips, only one can claim to be The Far Side’s deepest, and 45 years later, it remains unmatched.

“Thagomizer” was a word completely made up by Larson, with the implication being that Thag was impaled and killed by the spikes, thus resulting in the name “thagomizer.” However, what makes this strip so iconic is that the term “thagomizer” was actually adopted by the scientific community and is now used to refer to this part of a dinosaur’s tail.
